summary: Defines the Structure of Management Information for SNMPv2, the rules and notation used to describe the managed objects that SNMP can read and change. It was replaced by RFC 2578.

eli5.summary: Network devices keep lists of facts about themselves. This note sets the grammar for writing those lists, so every manager program can read them the same way.

subtitle: The rulebook for writing down what a network device can report and be told to change, in SNMPv2.

tldr.problem: Management stations and the devices they manage need a common, precise way to describe the managed objects (counters, tables, settings and alerts) that SNMP reads and changes.
tldr.mechanism: The SMI defines a restricted subset of ASN.1 plus macros (MODULE-IDENTITY, OBJECT-IDENTITY, OBJECT-TYPE, NOTIFICATION-TYPE), a set of base data types, and a naming tree rooted at the Internet subtree 1.3.6.1.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1902 was obsoleted by RFC 2578, which is the current form of the SMIv2 definitions. It had itself replaced RFC 1442.

today: RFC 1902 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2578, which is the current SMIv2 specification. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1442.

sections.title: What the SMI Is For
sections.content:
A management system has agents running on managed devices, at least one management station, and a protocol that carries management information between them. The information is viewed as a collection of managed objects living in a virtual store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Related objects are grouped into MIB modules.

MIB modules are written in an adapted subset of OSI's Abstract Syntax Notation One (ASN.1). The Structure of Management Information (SMI) defines that subset and assigns the administrative values that go with it. It has three parts: module definitions (the MODULE-IDENTITY macro), object definitions (OBJECT-TYPE) and notification definitions (NOTIFICATION-TYPE).

The RFC calls the earlier framework (RFCs 1155, 1157 and 1212) SNMPv1 and the framework it belongs to SNMPv2.
sections.eli5: Devices keep lists of facts about themselves. This note says exactly how to write those lists so any manager program can read them.

sections.title: Information Modules and Naming
sections.content:
An information module is an ASN.1 module that defines network management information. There are three kinds: MIB modules (objects and notifications), compliance statements, and capability statements for agent implementations. A standard module may not contain capability statements. Every module starts with exactly one MODULE-IDENTITY invocation, right after any IMPORTS, giving contact information and a revision history. Modules may not define new ASN.1 macros or use EXPORTS.

Each definition has the form descriptor macro clauses ::= value. A descriptor starts with a lower-case letter, has no hyphens, must be unique and mnemonic, and must not exceed 64 characters (over 32 is not recommended).

Every object is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER: an ordered list of non-negative sub-identifiers, at most 128 of them, each no greater than 4294967295. The Internet subtree is 1.3.6.1. Under it, mgmt(2) holds standard objects, experimental(3) holds objects being designed by IETF working groups, and private(4) with enterprises(1) beneath it holds objects defined unilaterally, such as vendor product models.
sections.eli5: Every fact gets an address made of numbers, like a street address that gets more specific with each number. Standard facts live on one street and company-specific facts live on another.

sections.title: Base Data Types
sections.content:
The SMI limits object values to a small set of base types.

  • Integer32: -2147483648 to 2147483647. Unsigned32: 0 to 4294967295.
  • OCTET STRING: binary or text data. Sizes over 255 octets may cause interoperability problems.
  • OBJECT IDENTIFIER and BITS (named bits numbered contiguously from zero).
  • IpAddress: an OCTET STRING of length 4 in network byte order, kept for historical reasons.
  • Counter32 rises until 4294967295 and then wraps to zero. A lone counter value has no meaning on its own, only the change between readings does. Counter64 works the same way up to 18446744073709551615 and may be used in standard modules only if a 32-bit counter would wrap in less than one hour.
  • Gauge32 can rise and fall but sticks at its maximum, at most 4294967295.
  • TimeTicks: hundredths of a second between two epochs.
  • Opaque: only for backward compatibility and not allowed on objects in standard MIB modules.

Counters may only be read-only or accessible-for-notify and may not have a DEFVAL.
sections.eli5: There is a small box of building blocks: whole numbers, text, addresses, counters that only go up, and gauges that go up and down like a thermometer. Everything has to be built from those.

sections.title: Defining Objects and Tables
sections.content:
The OBJECT-TYPE macro has required SYNTAX, MAX-ACCESS, STATUS and DESCRIPTION clauses, and optional UNITS, REFERENCE, INDEX or AUGMENTS, and DEFVAL clauses. MAX-ACCESS is the most access that makes protocol sense, and is one of not-accessible, accessible-for-notify, read-only, read-write or read-create. STATUS is current, deprecated or obsolete.

Management operations act only on scalar objects, but the SMI lets designers imagine conceptual tables: a table object of type SEQUENCE OF an entry type, containing a row object, which contains columnar objects. The INDEX clause says how to build the instance identifier for a row, for example one sub-identifier for an integer index, or the length followed by one sub-identifier per octet for a variable-length string. An AUGMENTS clause is the alternative when a new table has a one-to-one match with an existing one. Plain scalar objects are identified by appending a sub-identifier of zero.

Tables whose rows can be created or deleted should have a status column of type RowStatus with read-create access.
sections.eli5: A table is like a spreadsheet. The index says which row you mean, and each column is a different fact about that row. The rules also say who may look and who may change things.

sections.title: Notifications and Changing a Module
sections.content:
The NOTIFICATION-TYPE macro describes unsolicited reports, carried in a SNMPv2-Trap-PDU or InformRequest-PDU. An optional OBJECTS clause lists the objects included, none of which may be not-accessible. For newly defined notifications the next to last sub-identifier of the name must be zero, for compatibility with proxy agents. The RFC's example is a linkUp notification carrying ifIndex.

Modules can be revised. The MODULE-IDENTITY is updated with a new LAST-UPDATED and a REVISION clause, but the module name stays the same. Allowed object changes include adding enumerations, moving STATUS from current to deprecated to obsolete, adding DEFVAL, REFERENCE or UNITS clauses, adding columns at the end of a row, and defining new objects. Any other semantic change, including renaming a descriptor, requires a new OBJECT IDENTIFIER. Appendices cover converting ("de-OSIfying") MIB modules from other organizations and sub-typing rules.
sections.eli5: When a gadget has something important to say, like a link coming up, it can shout without being asked. And if you fix the labels later, you must not change what an old label means, or you must give it a new address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC's Security Considerations section is a single sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The SMI only defines notation and naming, so any protection comes from the other parts of the SNMPv2 framework. Note that MAX-ACCESS is independent of any administrative authorization policy.
sections.eli5: This note is only the rulebook for labels, so it says nothing about locks. Locks are handled elsewhere.

items.label: not-accessible
items.desc: Auxiliary object, such as a table or row.

items.label: read-write
items.desc: May be read and written, but not created.

items.label: read-create
items.desc: May be read, written and created.
